claims.text: Rapid-heating synthesis of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles typically produces phase separation.
Rapid-heating synthesis typically produces elemental or compositional inhomogeneity.
Rapid-heating synthesis typically produces uncontrolled or irregular particle morphology.
An intermediate isothermal hold at 500–600°C for 10–30 minutes enhances atomic diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Enhanced diffusion during the hold mitigates local compositional fluctuations.
Local compositional fluctuations promote phase separation and elemental segregation during rapid heating.
Mitigation of local compositional fluctuations enables stabilization of a single-phase solid solution.
The controlled process should use an inert atmosphere and a heating rate slower than that of the rapid-heating baseline.
The applicable compositional window has inter-element mixing enthalpies within ±10 kJ/mol.
Mixing enthalpies within ±10 kJ/mol make entropy stabilization viable in this system.
Rapid heating kinetically locks in local compositional fluctuations.
Locked-in compositional fluctuations favor nucleation of segregated phases.
A hold near the diffusion-onset temperature activates atomic mobility and permits more uniform redistribution of the constituent atoms.
More uniform atomic redistribution increases the configurational-entropy contribution.
The increased configurational-entropy contribution stabilizes a single-phase solid solution over multiphase or segregated structures.
Relative to rapid heating, the controlled thermal profile will produce greater phase uniformity and elemental homogeneity.
Relative to rapid heating, the controlled thermal profile will improve control of particle morphology.
Relative to rapid heating, the controlled thermal profile will reduce the tendency for high-temperature decomposition events.
Temperatures or dwell times insufficient to activate diffusion will fail to produce the proposed homogenization.
Excessive annealing can induce sintering and adverse morphological changes.
